overview: A series of Pacific systems keeps the West wet and unsettled through the holiday, with snow levels rising and falling with each front. Rocky Mountain resorts see mostly light snow and quiet driving before a Thursday system brings more. A powerful coastal storm hits the East on Thanksgiving.

regions.title: Cascades
regions.text: A series of frontal systems moves across Washington this week, with a wave of rain and mountain snow on Tuesday and Wednesday. Snow levels climb to around 5,000 feet at times, so rain mixes in at lower resorts. Crystal Mountain leads the region with 23 inches for the week, including a 9-inch day on Wednesday. Winds are strong from the south and southeast, with gusts near 45 mph.

regions.title: Coast Mountains
regions.text: Mild, wet air off the Pacific keeps British Columbia's coastal mountains in a rain-and-snow mix this week. Whistler's upper slopes get the best snow, with a 13-inch day forecast Wednesday, but Wednesday and Thursday are mostly rain. Cypress Mountain sees mainly rain after Monday. Freezing levels stay high, so the best snow sits above the base.

regions.title: Northern Rockies
regions.text: Dry, mild weather holds across western Wyoming and Montana through Wednesday. A new system arrives Thursday evening, bringing snow showers to western Wyoming and increasing travel impacts Friday into the weekend. The National Weather Service calls for more, 6 to 15 inches at Jackson Hole and 10 to 22 inches at Grand Targhee over Thanksgiving through Saturday night. Along the Montana Rocky Mountain Front, strong westerly winds and blowing snow are likely.

regions.title: Northeast
regions.text: A powerful coastal storm brings heavy rain, high winds and coastal flooding to the East Coast Wednesday through Friday, centered on Thanksgiving. Ontario's Blue Mountain and Quebec's Le Massif and Tremblant see a mix of flurries, freezing rain and rain, with the best accumulation Friday. A snow squall warning covers Blue Mountain from Tuesday.

sources.name: NOAA buoys 51001 / 51101 (method: Powder Buoy, Mike Ruzek)

buoy.text: Buoys 51001 and 51101 near Hawaii popped Nov 11, the swell signal Powder Buoy watches for a Wasatch storm about two weeks later — here Nov 22–28. In past winters a pop raised the chance of a Wasatch storm in that window by roughly 6 to 12 points. Experimental: promising, not proven.
